Point forecasts under heavy-tailed losses

A point forecast needs a target and a loss function. The mean, median, and an event probability summarize different aspects of a distribution. Binary calibration evaluates the last of these after an event has been specified. A single number leaves the probability of a large error and its consequences unspecified. Heavy tails make this omission particularly costly: the sample mean may converge slowly, and an average forecast score may lack the moments needed for its usual error bars. This note treats SCoFT v4 chapter 11, §11.4, pp. 231–235, and chapter 12, §§12.1–12.4, pp. 241–246 Taleb, 2025.

We prove the loss and transformation identities below, cite the general stable-limit theorem, and label simulated sampling quantiles as estimates. The pandemic discussion uses synthetic quantities; it does not estimate COVID-19 fatalities or evaluate a particular intervention.

Write d∈Rd\in\mathbb Rd∈R for a fixed point forecast and XXX for the future amount, following the shared notation. The expected loss evaluates the action ddd under a specified probability law. Estimating that law from observations is a further problem.

Which point minimizes expected loss?¶

We prove the squared- and absolute-loss claims at their finite-risk scope.

Proposition 1 (The mean uniquely minimizes finite expected squared loss)

Let XXX be real with EX2<∞\mathbb E X^2<\inftyEX2<∞ and μ=EX\mu=\mathbb E Xμ=EX. For every fixed d∈Rd\in\mathbb Rd∈R,

E[(X−d)2]=Var⁡(X)+(d−μ)2.\mathbb E[(X-d)^2] =\operatorname{Var}(X)+(d-\mu)^2.E[(X−d)2]=Var(X)+(d−μ)2.
(1)

The unique minimizing forecast is d=μd=\mud=μ.

Proof 1

Expand X−d=(X−μ)+(μ−d)X-d=(X-\mu)+(\mu-d)X−d=(X−μ)+(μ−d). The cross term vanishes because E(X−μ)=0\mathbb E(X-\mu)=0E(X−μ)=0. The remaining square (d−μ)2(d-\mu)^2(d−μ)2 is nonnegative and vanishes exactly at d=μd=\mud=μ.

Finite variance of the sample mean is not needed to define a population median, and existence of a population mean alone does not make the squared-loss objective finite.

Proposition 2 (Medians minimize finite expected absolute loss)

Let XXX be real with CDF FFF and E∣X∣<∞\mathbb E|X|<\inftyE∣X∣<∞. For any d2>d1d_2>d_1d2​>d1​,

E∣X−d2∣−E∣X−d1∣=∫d1d2{2F(t)−1} dt.\begin{aligned} &\mathbb E|X-d_2|-\mathbb E|X-d_1|\\ &\qquad=\int_{d_1}^{d_2}\{2F(t)-1\}\,dt. \end{aligned}​E∣X−d2​∣−E∣X−d1​∣=∫d1​d2​​{2F(t)−1}dt.​
(2)

The minimizing points are precisely the medians F(d−)≤1/2≤F(d)F(d-)\le1/2\le F(d)F(d−)≤1/2≤F(d), including atoms and nonunique medians.

Proof 2

Integrate the pointwise slopes of ∣x−d∣|x-d|∣x−d∣ in ddd. Their magnitude is at most one, so interchanging expectation and this finite integral is valid. The value of a slope exactly at an atom does not affect the integral. Monotonicity of FFF shows that the minimizing points are precisely the medians: F(d−)≤1/2≤F(d)F(d-)\le1/2\le F(d)F(d−)≤1/2≤F(d). This covers nonunique medians and atoms.

A median is a property of any real probability distribution; the preceding finite-expected-loss optimization requires the additional integrability assumption.

A finite point does not remove an infinite expected loss¶

The moment theorem gives a sharp boundary for exact Pareto losses.

Proposition 3 (Moment boundaries for Pareto forecast errors)

Let XXX be exact Pareto Type I with xm>0x_m>0xm​>0 and α>0\alpha>0α>0. For each fixed d∈Rd\in\mathbb Rd∈R,

E∣X−d∣<∞⟺α>1,E[(X−d)2]<∞⟺α>2.\begin{gathered} \mathbb E|X-d|<\infty \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\alpha>1,\\ \mathbb E[(X-d)^2]<\infty \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\alpha>2. \end{gathered}E∣X−d∣<∞⟺α>1,E[(X−d)2]<∞⟺α>2.​
(3)
Proof 3

To prove necessity, for X>2∣d∣X>2|d|X>2∣d∣ the absolute error is at least X/2X/2X/2. The tail integral of the corresponding power diverges at and below the moment boundary. For sufficiency use ∣X−d∣≤X+∣d∣|X-d|\le X+|d|∣X−d∣≤X+∣d∣ and (X−d)2≤2X2+2d2(X-d)^2\le2X^2+2d^2(X−d)2≤2X2+2d2.

Thus every finite point has infinite squared risk when 1<α≤21<\alpha\le21<α≤2, even though a finite mean exists. One can compare suitable differences of losses under weaker conditions, but that is a different optimization formulation; it is not a finite minimum of the ordinary squared-risk objective.

Proposition 4 (Exact absolute risk under a Pareto law)

For exact Pareto XXX with xm>0x_m>0xm​>0 and α>1\alpha>1α>1, the mean and median are

μ=αxmα−1,median⁡(X)=xm21/α.\mu=\frac{\alpha x_m}{\alpha-1}, \qquad \operatorname{median}(X)=x_m2^{1/\alpha}.μ=α−1αxm​​,median(X)=xm​21/α.
(4)

For d≥xmd\ge x_md≥xm​,

E∣X−d∣=d−μ+2xmαd1−αα−1.\mathbb E|X-d| =d-\mu+\frac{2x_m^\alpha d^{1-\alpha}}{\alpha-1}.E∣X−d∣=d−μ+α−12xmα​d1−α​.
(5)
Proof 4

The mean is the Pareto moment formula, and the median satisfies F(xm21/α)=1/2F(x_m2^{1/\alpha})=1/2F(xm​21/α)=1/2. Apply the identity ∣X−d∣=d−X+2(X−d)+|X-d|=d-X+2(X-d)_+∣X−d∣=d−X+2(X−d)+​ and the excess-mean formula to obtain the expected absolute loss.

This finite expression permits an exact comparison; a finite Monte Carlo average cannot prove that an expected loss exists.

Use pareto_tail_bet for the excess mean and point_forecast_loss for observed errors. The simulation uses exact Pareto draws at α=1.5,xm=1\alpha=1.5,x_m=1α=1.5,xm​=1, PCG64 seed 1110, and 20,000 observations. It has a finite absolute-risk target and an infinite squared-risk target.

Code: exact absolute risk and finite simulated losses
import numpy as np
from xmath.incerto.calibration import pareto_tail_bet, point_forecast_loss

alpha, xm = 1.5, 1.0
mean = alpha * xm / (alpha - 1)
median = xm * 2**(1 / alpha)
rng = np.random.default_rng(1110)
x = xm * (1 + rng.pareto(alpha, 20000))
for label, d in (("median", median), ("mean", mean)):
    excess = pareto_tail_bet(alpha, d, xm=xm)["excess_mean"]
    risk = d - mean + 2 * excess
    print(f"{label}: point={d:.3f}, exact absolute risk={risk:.3f}")
    print(f"  sample absolute={point_forecast_loss(x, d).mean():.3f}")
    squared = point_forecast_loss(x, d, metric="squared").mean()
    print(f"  sample squared={squared:.3f}; population squared=inf")

Output

median: point=1.587, exact absolute risk=1.762
  sample absolute=1.702
  sample squared=80.337; population squared=inf
mean: point=3.000, exact absolute risk=2.309
  sample absolute=2.252
  sample squared=78.520; population squared=inf

The moment-estimation note distinguishes existence of an estimand from finite variance of its estimator. That distinction also applies to losses: iid averages of integrable absolute errors can be consistent even when their sampling variance is infinite.

Normalization changes the score’s tail¶

Absolute error, squared error, MASE, and sMAPE are different functions of the same forecast and outcome.

Proposition 5 (Tails of Pareto absolute and squared forecast errors)

Let XXX be exact Pareto Type I with xm>0x_m>0xm​>0, α>0\alpha>0α>0, and fix d∈Rd\in\mathbb Rd∈R. Write Fˉ(t)=P(X>t)\bar F(t)=P(X>t)Fˉ(t)=P(X>t). For sufficiently large ttt,

P(∣X−d∣>t)=Fˉ(t+d),P((X−d)2>t)=Fˉ(t+d).\begin{gathered} P(|X-d|>t)=\bar F(t+d),\\ P((X-d)^2>t)=\bar F(\sqrt t+d). \end{gathered}P(∣X−d∣>t)=Fˉ(t+d),P((X−d)2>t)=Fˉ(t​+d).​
(6)

The absolute and squared errors have regularly varying tails with exponents α\alphaα and α/2\alpha/2α/2, respectively. For any fixed s0>0s_0>0s0​>0, ∣X−d∣/s0|X-d|/s_0∣X−d∣/s0​ also has tail exponent α\alphaα.

Proof 5

For the first identity, t>∣d∣t>|d|t>∣d∣ eliminates the lower branch X<d−tX<d-tX<d−t; for the second use t>∣d∣\sqrt t>|d|t​>∣d∣. Once the remaining thresholds exceed xmx_mxm​, the Pareto formula applies. Taking ratios as t→∞t\to\inftyt→∞ shows tail exponents α\alphaα and α/2\alpha/2α/2, respectively. Replacing ttt by s0ts_0ts0​t in the absolute-error survival preserves its regular-variation exponent.

Squaring the error changes its moment requirements.

MASE divides absolute error by a positive training-sample scale s0s_0s0​ Hyndman & Koehler, 2006, author manuscript §3, pp. 12–13. For a fixed realized s0>0s_0>0s0​>0, it preserves the absolute error’s tail exponent. If that scale is random, a conditional statement given training data does not automatically extend to the unconditional ratio: values near zero can change its moments. A constant training series can give s0=0s_0=0s0​=0, requiring an explicit policy before scoring.

For a fixed training vector y1,…,ymy_1,\ldots,y_my1​,…,ym​ and seasonal lag h<mh<mh<m, a conventional scale is the mean of ∣yj−yj−h∣|y_j-y_{j-h}|∣yj​−yj−h​∣ over j=h+1,…,mj=h+1,\ldots,mj=h+1,…,m. It is a naive forecast’s training error, not the dispersion of future observations around their sample mean. The helper accepts the scale explicitly, so the chosen lag and training window remain visible.

Several denominator conventions have been called sMAPE Hyndman, 2014. The convention used here is

2∣x−d∣∣x∣+∣d∣,∣x∣+∣d∣>0,\frac{2|x-d|}{|x|+|d|},\qquad |x|+|d|>0,∣x∣+∣d∣2∣x−d∣​,∣x∣+∣d∣>0,
(7)

with score zero when d=x=0d=x=0d=x=0.

Proposition 6 (Boundedness of the stated sMAPE score)

For every x,d∈Rx,d\in\mathbb Rx,d∈R, the score 2∣x−d∣/(∣x∣+∣d∣)2|x-d|/(|x|+|d|)2∣x−d∣/(∣x∣+∣d∣), defined as zero when x=d=0x=d=0x=d=0, lies in [0,2][0,2][0,2].

Proof 6

When the denominator is positive, use ∣x−d∣≤∣x∣+∣d∣|x-d|\le|x|+|d|∣x−d∣≤∣x∣+∣d∣. The zero-denominator convention also lies in the stated interval.

A percentage presentation multiplies this by 100. Thus this normalized score is bounded even for unbounded XXX. A statement that every M4-style score has the same tail class as the underlying amount would be false for this sMAPE. The source’s §11.4 formula also needs absolute values in its numerator to describe either of these absolute-error metrics: signed errors can cancel. The chosen zero convention is stated explicitly, rather than evaluating 0/00/00/0.

Use point_forecast_loss. The outputs show how bounded normalization can hide changes in magnitude.

from xmath.incerto.calibration import point_forecast_loss

for metric in ("absolute", "squared", "smape"):
    values = point_forecast_loss([0, 10, 10000], 0, metric=metric)
    print(metric + ": " + ", ".join(f"{v:.2f}" for v in values))
try:
    point_forecast_loss([1, 2], 1, metric="mase", scale=0)
except ValueError as error:
    print(type(error).__name__ + ": " + str(error))

Output

absolute: 0.00, 10.00, 10000.00
squared: 0.00, 100.00, 100000000.00
smape: 0.00, 2.00, 2.00
ValueError: MASE requires a positive finite training scale

Forecast accuracy and the decision¶

Changing the score can change the preferred point and the sampling uncertainty. It does not by itself specify a useful action. A probability forecast may guide a threshold decision; an amount forecast may guide capacity; an explicit nonlinear payoff may require several parts of the predictive distribution. The hinge representation and payoff identity show how to evaluate a stated exposure when the required expectations exist. None of these arguments says that every point forecast of a heavy-tailed variable is meaningless.

For an event score, reporting the conditional probability minimizes expected Brier loss. For absolute amount error, a median minimizes finite expected loss. For squared amount error, the mean does so when the second moment is finite. These are separate statements with separate domains.

Estimating a mean and predicting an outcome¶

Even when the training mean consistently estimates μ\muμ, the future amount remains random.

Proposition 7 (Estimation and prediction have different errors)

Let X1,X2,…X_1,X_2,\ldotsX1​,X2​,… be iid with a nondegenerate real law XXX satisfying E∣X∣<∞\mathbb E|X|<\inftyE∣X∣<∞. Set μ=EX\mu=\mathbb E Xμ=EX and Xˉn=n−1∑i=1nXi\bar X_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nX_iXˉn​=n−1∑i=1n​Xi​; Xn+1X_{n+1}Xn+1​ is independent of the training sample. Then Xn+1−Xˉn⇒X−μX_{n+1}-\bar X_n\Rightarrow X-\muXn+1​−Xˉn​⇒X−μ. If also σ2=Var⁡(X)<∞\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(X)<\inftyσ2=Var(X)<∞,

Var⁡(Xˉn)=σ2/n,Var⁡(Xn+1−Xˉn)=σ2(1+1/n).\begin{gathered} \operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n)=\sigma^2/n,\\ \operatorname{Var}(X_{n+1}-\bar X_n) =\sigma^2(1+1/n). \end{gathered}Var(Xˉn​)=σ2/n,Var(Xn+1​−Xˉn​)=σ2(1+1/n).​
(8)
Proof 7

The iid law of large numbers gives Xˉn→μ\bar X_n\to\muXˉn​→μ in probability. Slutsky’s theorem, applied to the unchanged marginal law of Xn+1X_{n+1}Xn+1​, gives the distributional limit. In the finite-variance case, independence makes the variance of the sum of the nnn observations equal to nσ2n\sigma^2nσ2. Dividing by n2n^2n2 gives the first variance. Independence of Xn+1X_{n+1}Xn+1​ and Xˉn\bar X_nXˉn​ gives the second by adding their variances.

The distinction matters before choosing a heavy-tail model. More training data can reduce estimation error while leaving substantial outcome risk.

For an exact scaling benchmark, take symmetric stable observations.

Eeit(Xi−μ)=e−∣σt∣α,t∈R.\mathbb E e^{it(X_i-\mu)} =e^{-|\sigma t|^\alpha},\qquad t\in\mathbb R.Eeit(Xi​−μ)=e−∣σt∣α,t∈R.
(9)

Xˉn−μ =d snZα,sn=σn1/α−1.\bar X_n-\mu\ \overset d=\ s_n Z_\alpha, \qquad s_n=\sigma n^{1/\alpha-1}.Xˉn​−μ =d sn​Zα​,sn​=σn1/α−1.
(10)

For every 0<r<s<10<r<s<10<r<s<1, the difference between the sss- and rrr-quantiles of Xˉn\bar X_nXˉn​ is sns_nsn​ times the corresponding width of ZαZ_\alphaZα​.

Proof 8

Multiply characteristic functions at t/nt/nt/n:

Eeit(Xˉn−μ)=e−n∣σt/n∣α,sn=σn1/α−1,Xˉn−μ =d snZα.\begin{gathered} \mathbb E e^{it(\bar X_n-\mu)} =e^{-n|\sigma t/n|^\alpha},\\ s_n=\sigma n^{1/\alpha-1},\\ \bar X_n-\mu\ \overset d=\ s_n Z_\alpha. \end{gathered}Eeit(Xˉn​−μ)=e−n∣σt/n∣α,sn​=σn1/α−1,Xˉn​−μ =d sn​Zα​.​
(11)

Equality of characteristic functions gives the distributional identity. Quantiles shift by μ\muμ and scale by the positive number sns_nsn​, so their differences have the stated scaling.

Here μ\muμ denotes a location, and is a population mean only for α>1\alpha>1α>1. At α=2\alpha=2α=2 the variance is 2σ22\sigma^22σ2. Every fixed interquantile width scales by sns_nsn​, including when moments do not exist. For 1<α<21<\alpha<21<α<2 the width shrinks more slowly than n−1/2n^{-1/2}n−1/2; for the Cauchy case α=1\alpha=1α=1 it stays constant; below one it increases. Symmetric stable variables can be negative, so this benchmark is an error model, not a literal fatality model.

Use stable_average_scale, the existing symmetric_stable_mean_abs, and stable_kappa. The scale exists throughout the grid; finite absolute error and kappa do not.

from xmath.incerto.forecasting import stable_average_scale
from xmath.incerto.limits import symmetric_stable_mean_abs
from xmath.incerto.concentration import stable_kappa

for alpha in (.8, 1, 1.5, 2):
    scale = stable_average_scale(alpha, 100)
    mad = symmetric_stable_mean_abs(alpha, n=100)
    kappa = stable_kappa(alpha)
    print(f"alpha={alpha:g}: scale={scale:.3f}, MAD={mad:.3f}, kappa={kappa:.3f}")

alpha=2: scale=0.100, MAD=0.113, kappa=0.000

The exact identity applies to stable parents. For iid exact positive Pareto observations, the attraction normalization requires a separate calculation.

For a nonnegative Pareto law with 0<α<10<\alpha<10<α<1, use zero centering; Xˉn/(xmn1/α−1)\bar X_n/(x_m n^{1/\alpha-1})Xˉn​/(xm​n1/α−1) has a nondegenerate positive stable limit. There is no finite mean to forecast. The following supporting result also applies to the nonnegative scores considered below.

Lemma 2 (Iid averages of nonnegative variables with infinite mean)

Let X1,X2,…X_1,X_2,\ldotsX1​,X2​,… be iid nonnegative random variables with EX1=∞\mathbb E X_1=\inftyEX1​=∞. Then n−1∑i=1nXi→∞n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\to\inftyn−1∑i=1n​Xi​→∞ almost surely.

Proof 10

Apply the bounded iid strong law to min⁡(Xi,b)\min(X_i,b)min(Xi​,b) for every positive integer bbb. On the intersection of these countably many probability-one events, the liminf of the original averages is at least Emin⁡(X1,b)\mathbb E\min(X_1,b)Emin(X1​,b) for every bbb. Monotone convergence sends these expectations to infinity.

Thus exact Pareto sample means diverge almost surely when α≤1\alpha\le1α≤1. At the exact Pareto boundary α=1\alpha=1α=1, Durrett’s constants are an=xmna_n=x_m nan​=xm​n and bn=xmnlog⁡nb_n=x_m n\log nbn​=xm​nlogn. His centered stable limit thus applies to Xˉn/xm−log⁡n\bar X_n/x_m-\log nXˉn​/xm​−logn. The separate truncation argument gives Xˉn/(xmlog⁡n)→1\bar X_n/(x_m\log n)\to1Xˉn​/(xm​logn)→1 in probability. This positive-law boundary is different from the symmetric Cauchy location example. At a regular-variation moment boundary, the slowly varying factor can change integrability; these boundary conclusions use exact Pareto laws.

For α>2\alpha>2α>2, a Pareto mean has the ordinary finite-variance CLT. At α=2\alpha=2α=2 its infinite variance requires a logarithmic adjustment to Gaussian normalization. Neither case follows by extending the α<2\alpha<2α<2 stable power formula. There is no universal impossibility threshold at α=2.5\alpha=2.5α=2.5; a practical sample size requires a stated loss, tolerance, body, scale, and dependence model. See kappa for finite-sample absolute-error comparisons.

Why a forecast leaderboard can move¶

Evaluate a fixed forecast ddd on iid test observations using the average of the losses at (d,Xi)(d,X_i)(d,Xi​).

Corollary 1 (Moment thresholds for Pareto forecast scores)

Let XXX be exact Pareto Type I with xm>0x_m>0xm​>0, α>0\alpha>0α>0, and fix d∈Rd\in\mathbb Rd∈R. The finite-moment conditions for the indicated scores are exactly those in the table, using the sMAPE convention above.

ScoreFinite expected scoreFinite score variance
Absolute errorα>1\alpha>1α>1α>2\alpha>2α>2
Squared errorα>2\alpha>2α>2α>4\alpha>4α>4
Our sMAPE conventionEvery α>0\alpha>0α>0Every α>0\alpha>0α>0
Proof 11

The comparison in Proposition 3 applies to the first, second, and fourth powers of ∣X−d∣|X-d|∣X−d∣: for sufficiently large XXX, X/2≤∣X−d∣≤X+∣d∣X/2\le|X-d|\le X+|d|X/2≤∣X−d∣≤X+∣d∣. The Pareto moment test therefore gives the boundaries for each loss and its square. The sMAPE conclusion follows from Proposition 6.

The earlier tail calculation gives exponents α\alphaα for absolute error and α/2\alpha/2α/2 for squared error. If a nonnegative score has infinite expectation, its iid average diverges almost surely by Lemma 2. If its mean is finite but its variance infinite, the strong law still applies; the usual variance-based standard error lacks its population justification. In particular, finite variance of XXX is insufficient for a conventional CLT for the squared score. An RMSE transformation does not restore a missing population MSE.

Paired comparisons can behave better than either score separately.

Proposition 9 (Bounded paired differences of absolute losses)

For any real random variable XXX and fixed d1,d2∈Rd_1,d_2\in\mathbb Rd1​,d2​∈R,

∣∣X−d1∣−∣X−d2∣∣≤∣d1−d2∣.\bigl||X-d_1|-|X-d_2|\bigr| \le |d_1-d_2|.∣∣​∣X−d1​∣−∣X−d2​∣∣∣​≤∣d1​−d2​∣.
(15)

Consequently the paired difference has finite mean and variance even when both expected absolute scores are infinite. Its iid sample average satisfies the ordinary finite-variance CLT, allowing zero variance.

Proof 12

The reverse triangle inequality gives the bound. Boundedness supplies the moments required by the iid CLT.

Proposition 10 (Paired differences of squared losses)

For any real random variable XXX and fixed d1,d2∈Rd_1,d_2\in\mathbb Rd1​,d2​∈R,

(X−d1)2−(X−d2)2=2(d2−d1)X+d12−d22.\begin{aligned} &(X-d_1)^2-(X-d_2)^2\\ &\quad=2(d_2-d_1)X+d_1^2-d_2^2. \end{aligned}​(X−d1​)2−(X−d2​)2=2(d2​−d1​)X+d12​−d22​.​
(16)

If XXX is exact Pareto with xm>0x_m>0xm​>0, α>0\alpha>0α>0, and d1≠d2d_1\ne d_2d1​=d2​, the difference has a finite mean exactly when α>1\alpha>1α>1 and finite variance exactly when α>2\alpha>2α>2.

Proof 13

Expand both squares and cancel X2X^2X2. When d1≠d2d_1\ne d_2d1​=d2​, the result is a nonconstant affine function of XXX. The Pareto first- and second-moment criteria give the stated boundaries.

A consistent strict paired ranking is therefore possible when the expected loss difference is nonzero, even when individual MSEs are infinite; it compares an integrable difference, not two finite expected scores. For either paired comparison, a zero expected loss difference is a tie in expectation, whatever the sample averages show. Time-varying forecasts, training selection, dependence, and model changes require their own analysis. These identities do not validate an arbitrary leaderboard or establish that all forecasting comparisons fail.

Use pareto_forecast_scores. Each replication evaluates the fixed median forecast on fresh test data. All samples and scores are retained; the helper raises on numerical overflow.

Code: repeated evaluation of one forecast
import numpy as np
from xmath.incerto.forecasting import pareto_forecast_scores

for n in (30, 300, 3000):
    samples = pareto_forecast_scores(1.5, n, 2**(2/3),
                                     repetitions=2000, seed=1210+n)
    print(f"n={n}")
    for metric in ("absolute", "squared", "smape"):
        quantiles = np.quantile(samples[metric], [.1, .5, .9])
        print(f"  {metric}: " + ", ".join(f"{v:.3f}" for v in quantiles))

Output

  absolute: 0.724, 1.264, 2.743
  squared: 1.410, 7.047, 62.107
  smape: 0.329, 0.411, 0.504
n=300
  absolute: 1.199, 1.542, 2.314
  squared: 8.512, 23.456, 170.817
  smape: 0.388, 0.415, 0.442
n=3000
  absolute: 1.485, 1.669, 2.035
  squared: 26.927, 62.111, 414.730
  smape: 0.406, 0.415, 0.424

Predictive ranges and tail payoffs¶

For 0<τ<10<\tau<10<τ<1, define the quantile loss

ℓτ(d,x)=(τ−1{x<d})(x−d).\ell_\tau(d,x) =(\tau-\mathbf1_{\{x<d\}})(x-d).ℓτ​(d,x)=(τ−1{x<d}​)(x−d).
(17)
Proposition 11 (Quantile loss and its paired differences)

Let XXX be real with CDF FFF, fix 0<τ<10<\tau<10<τ<1, and define ℓτ(d,x)=(τ−1{x<d})(x−d)\ell_\tau(d,x)=(\tau-\mathbf1_{\{x<d\}})(x-d)ℓτ​(d,x)=(τ−1{x<d}​)(x−d). For d2>d1d_2>d_1d2​>d1​, the paired difference is bounded in absolute value by ∣d2−d1∣|d_2-d_1|∣d2​−d1​∣ and satisfies

E[ℓτ(d2,X)−ℓτ(d1,X)]=∫d1d2{F(t)−τ} dt.\mathbb E[\ell_\tau(d_2,X)-\ell_\tau(d_1,X)] =\int_{d_1}^{d_2}\{F(t)-\tau\}\,dt.E[ℓτ​(d2​,X)−ℓτ​(d1​,X)]=∫d1​d2​​{F(t)−τ}dt.
(18)

If E∣X∣<∞\mathbb E|X|<\inftyE∣X∣<∞, each expected loss is finite, the left side also equals the difference of expectations, and the minimizers are precisely the τ\tauτ-quantiles F(d−)≤τ≤F(d)F(d-)\le\tau\le F(d)F(d−)≤τ≤F(d).

Proof 14

The pointwise slope in ddd is 1{x<d}−τ\mathbf1_{\{x<d\}}-\tau1{x<d}​−τ away from d=xd=xd=x, with absolute value at most one. Integrate the slopes and use Fubini on the finite interval. Atom values do not affect the integral, so F(t−)F(t-)F(t−) may be replaced by F(t)F(t)F(t). If E∣X∣<∞\mathbb E|X|<\inftyE∣X∣<∞, both expected losses are finite and

Eℓτ(d2,X)−Eℓτ(d1,X)=∫d1d2{F(t)−τ} dt.\begin{aligned} &\mathbb E\ell_\tau(d_2,X) -\mathbb E\ell_\tau(d_1,X)\\ &\qquad=\int_{d_1}^{d_2}\{F(t)-\tau\}\,dt. \end{aligned}​Eℓτ​(d2​,X)−Eℓτ​(d1​,X)=∫d1​d2​​{F(t)−τ}dt.​
(19)

The minimizers are precisely the τ\tauτ-quantiles satisfying F(d−)≤τ≤F(d)F(d-)\le\tau\le F(d)F(d−)≤τ≤F(d) by monotonicity of FFF.

Without integrability, quantiles still exist, and expected paired differences remain finite because their magnitude is at most ∣d2−d1∣|d_2-d_1|∣d2​−d1​∣. The same integral then describes those differences; it must not be read as subtraction of two infinite expectations. A strict preference requires a nonzero expected paired loss difference; zero means a tie in expectation, whatever the sample averages show.

Proposition 12 (Finite quantiles of an exact Pareto law)

Let XXX be exact Pareto with xm>0x_m>0xm​>0 and α>0\alpha>0α>0. For every 0<τ<10<\tau<10<τ<1, its unique τ\tauτ-quantile is

qτ=xm(1−τ)−1/α.q_\tau=x_m(1-\tau)^{-1/\alpha}.qτ​=xm​(1−τ)−1/α.
(20)
Proof 15

Solve 1−(xm/qτ)α=τ1-(x_m/q_\tau)^\alpha=\tau1−(xm​/qτ​)α=τ; the CDF is continuous and strictly increasing on [xm,∞)[x_m,\infty)[xm​,∞).

For α=0.8,xm=1\alpha=0.8,x_m=1α=0.8,xm​=1, both a median and a 99th percentile are finite despite the infinite mean. The interval between any two specified quantiles has its stated probability under the continuous known model. Fitting that model introduces additional uncertainty. Compare finite quantiles using pareto_type1 and observed losses using quantile_loss.

from xmath.incerto.distributions import pareto_type1
from xmath.incerto.forecasting import quantile_loss

law = pareto_type1(.8)
print("quantiles: " + ", ".join(f"{v:.2f}" for v in law.ppf([.5, .9, .99])))
print(f"mean: {law.mean():.2f}")
values = quantile_loss([1, 3, 20], 3, tau=.9)
print("observed losses: " + ", ".join(f"{v:.2f}" for v in values))

Output

quantiles: 2.38, 17.78, 316.23
mean: inf
observed losses: 0.20, 0.00, 15.30

One quantile or one event probability still omits severity beyond the threshold.

Proposition 13 (Expected excess integrates the whole survival tail)

For a nonnegative random variable XXX, u∈Ru\in\mathbb Ru∈R, and Fˉ(t)=P(X>t)\bar F(t)=P(X>t)Fˉ(t)=P(X>t), with infinite values allowed,

E[(X−u)+]=∫u∞Fˉ(t) dt.\mathbb E[(X-u)_+] =\int_u^\infty\bar F(t)\,dt.E[(X−u)+​]=∫u∞​Fˉ(t)dt.
(21)
Proof 16

Apply Tonelli’s theorem to (X−u)+=∫u∞1{X>t} dt(X-u)_+=\int_u^\infty\mathbf1_{\{X>t\}}\,dt(X−u)+​=∫u∞​1{X>t}​dt.

Thus the whole survival curve determines expected excess; its value at one threshold does not. The counting-exceedances result, cited here, gives the following comparison: for nnn iid observations and a fixed threshold uuu, the empirical fraction exceeding uuu has variance Fˉ(u){1−Fˉ(u)}/n\bar F(u)\{1-\bar F(u)\}/nFˉ(u){1−Fˉ(u)}/n, where Fˉ(u)=P(X>u)\bar F(u)=P(X>u)Fˉ(u)=P(X>u), regardless of the amount’s moments. Its RMSE is of order n−1/2n^{-1/2}n−1/2 when 0<Fˉ(u)<10<\bar F(u)<10<Fˉ(u)<1; its MSE is of order n−1n^{-1}n−1, not o(n−1)o(n^{-1})o(n−1). For rare events its relative RMSE is {1−Fˉ(u)}/{nFˉ(u)}\sqrt{\{1-\bar F(u)\}/\{n\bar F(u)\}}{1−Fˉ(u)}/{nFˉ(u)}​, which can be large. See counting exceedances and tail beyond the sample for the proofs and limits.

A population cap and a log transform answer different questions¶

For fatalities in a fixed population over a fixed horizon, a deterministic population bound HHH implies 0≤X≤H0\le X\le H0≤X≤H, hence every positive moment is finite. An unbounded Pareto model can approximate an intermediate range, but an exponent below one cannot establish an infinite physical mean under that bound. Pooling events across changing populations also changes the model.

A cap alone need not make a sample informative about rare, severe losses.

Proposition 14 (Mean of a capped Pareto variable)

Let VVV be an unbounded exact Pareto variable with exponent α>0\alpha>0α>0 and minimum xm>0x_m>0xm​>0. In this capped model, XXX now denotes min⁡(V,H)\min(V,H)min(V,H), with xm≤H<∞x_m\le H<\inftyxm​≤H<∞. Then

EX=xm+xmα∫xmHt−α dt.\mathbb E X =x_m+x_m^\alpha\int_{x_m}^{H}t^{-\alpha}\,dt.EX=xm​+xmα​∫xm​H​t−αdt.
(22)

For α≠1\alpha\ne1α=1 this is

EX=xm(1+(H/xm)1−α−11−α).\mathbb E X =x_m\left(1+\frac{(H/x_m)^{1-\alpha}-1}{1-\alpha}\right).EX=xm​(1+1−α(H/xm​)1−α−1​).
(23)

At α=1\alpha=1α=1 it is xm{1+log⁡(H/xm)}x_m\{1+\log(H/x_m)\}xm​{1+log(H/xm​)}.

Proof 17

The survival-integral calculation in the LLN note integrates one below xmx_mxm​ and (xm/t)α(x_m/t)^\alpha(xm​/t)α from xmx_mxm​ to HHH. Evaluate that integral as a power when α≠1\alpha\ne1α=1 and a logarithm when α=1\alpha=1α=1.

For α<1\alpha<1α<1 this mean grows as a power of the remote cap. The iid bounded strong law holds at every fixed HHH; no cap-independent sample size follows. Capping creates an atom at HHH, and differs from conditioning VVV to fall below HHH.

Two logarithms have different purposes.

Proposition 15 (Logarithmic excesses of an exact Pareto variable)

If VVV is exact Pareto with xm>0x_m>0xm​>0 and α>0\alpha>0α>0, then log⁡(V/xm)\log(V/x_m)log(V/xm​) is exponential with rate α\alphaα.

Proof 18

For z≥0z\ge0z≥0, P(log⁡(V/xm)>z)=P(V>xmez)=e−αzP(\log(V/x_m)>z)=P(V>x_m e^z)=e^{-\alpha z}P(log(V/xm​)>z)=P(V>xm​ez)=e−αz.

This explains why log spacings can support Hill estimation while the raw sample mean is erratic. It does not recover raw expected harm by exponentiating a log mean; nonlinear expectations require the full law.

For any bounded variable 0≤X≤H0\le X\le H0≤X≤H with 0<H<∞0<H<\infty0<H<∞, an endpoint-removing dual transform is a separate modeling device.

Proposition 16 (Bounded-to-dual transformation and its inverse)

Fix 0<H<∞0<H<\infty0<H<∞. The increasing map from [0,H][0,H][0,H] to [0,∞][0,\infty][0,∞] and its inverse are

Z=−Hlog⁡(1−X/H),X=H(1−e−Z/H).\begin{gathered} Z=-H\log(1-X/H),\\ X=H(1-e^{-Z/H}). \end{gathered}Z=−Hlog(1−X/H),X=H(1−e−Z/H).​
(24)

Use Z=∞Z=\inftyZ=∞ at X=HX=HX=H and e−∞=0e^{-\infty}=0e−∞=0. As X/H→0X/H\to0X/H→0, Z=X+X2/(2H)+O(X3/H2)Z=X+X^2/(2H)+O(X^3/H^2)Z=X+X2/(2H)+O(X3/H2). For every law of ZZZ on [0,∞][0,\infty][0,∞], the inverse has mean E[H(1−e−Z/H)]≤H\mathbb E[H(1-e^{-Z/H})]\le HE[H(1−e−Z/H)]≤H, regardless of whether EZ\mathbb E ZEZ is finite.

Proof 19

The forward map is increasing on 0≤X<H0\le X<H0≤X<H, maps zero to zero, and tends to infinity at HHH. Solving the equation gives its inverse. For X/H→0X/H\to0X/H→0, Taylor expansion gives Z=X+X2/(2H)+O(X3/H2)Z=X+X^2/(2H)+O(X^3/H^2)Z=X+X2/(2H)+O(X3/H2). At X=HX=HX=H, use the extended dual value Z=∞Z=\inftyZ=∞. The inverse takes values in [0,H][0,H][0,H], so its expectation is bounded by HHH.

Ordinary-scale observations move little. An endpoint atom remains an atom at infinity; finite dual-tail modeling requires handling it explicitly.

An increasing transformation preserves quantiles, not means. To obtain an expectation in physical units from an assumed dual law, evaluate E[H(1−e−Z/H)]\mathbb E[H(1-e^{-Z/H})]E[H(1−e−Z/H)], which is at most HHH, even if EZ=∞\mathbb E Z=\inftyEZ=∞. A heavy dual tail is an assumption to check, not a consequence of the transformation. This is the zero-lower-endpoint special case of the construction discussed by Cirillo and Taleb Cirillo & Taleb, 2020, §II, p. 4; no fitted shadow mean is computed here.

Use bounded_to_dual and dual_to_bounded. The endpoint and invalid-input behavior are included.

Code: endpoint transformation and inverse
from xmath.incerto.forecasting import bounded_to_dual, dual_to_bounded

for x in (0, 1, 50, 99, 100):
    z = bounded_to_dual(x, upper=100)
    back = dual_to_bounded(z, upper=100)
    print(f"x={x}: dual={z:.3f}, inverse={back:.3f}")
for x in (101, float("nan")):
    try:
        bounded_to_dual(x, upper=100)
    except ValueError as error:
        print(type(error).__name__ + ": " + str(error))

Output

x=0: dual=0.000, inverse=0.000
x=1: dual=1.005, inverse=1.000
x=50: dual=69.315, inverse=50.000
x=99: dual=460.517, inverse=99.000
x=100: dual=inf, inverse=100.000
ValueError: values must lie in [0, upper]
ValueError: values must contain finite values

Pandemic tails, action, and conditional forecasts¶

SCoFT v4 §12.2, p. 242, refers to heavy tails in historical epidemic fatalities. The underlying study fits historical event totals and a bounded transformation Cirillo & Taleb, 2020, §§II–IV, pp. 2–6. This is empirical model evidence, not a theorem that each disease, country, or future wave has an unbounded Pareto law. Event definitions, missing episodes, uncertain death counts, changing population, and interventions matter when applying that inference. A tail parameter estimated across historical events is not automatically a time-series parameter within one outbreak.

Data-source note. The cited study describes its historical compilation in §II and Table I. We do not import, redistribute, or refit that table. Every numerical example on this page is synthetic.

Multiplicative growth can amplify parameter uncertainty without proving a power law. The following calculation uses a deliberately simple rate model.

Proposition 17 (Exponential growth with an exponential random rate)

Fix t>0t>0t>0, x0>0x_0>0x0​>0, and let RRR be exponential with rate λ>0\lambda>0λ>0. Then X=x0etRX=x_0e^{tR}X=x0​etR is exact Pareto with cutoff x0x_0x0​ and exponent α=λ/t\alpha=\lambda/tα=λ/t: P(X>x)=(x/x0)−λ/tP(X>x)=(x/x_0)^{-\lambda/t}P(X>x)=(x/x0​)−λ/t for x≥x0x\ge x_0x≥x0​.

Proof 20

For x≥x0x\ge x_0x≥x0​,

P(X>x)=P ⁣(R>log⁡(x/x0)t)=(x/x0)−λ/t.\begin{aligned} P(X>x) &=P\!\left(R>\frac{\log(x/x_0)}{t}\right)\\ &=(x/x_0)^{-\lambda/t}. \end{aligned}P(X>x)​=P(R>tlog(x/x0​)​)=(x/x0​)−λ/t.​
(25)

Also R≥0R\ge0R≥0 ensures X≥x0X\ge x_0X≥x0​.

A normal RRR gives a lognormal amount instead; deterministic exponential growth is not by itself mathematical chaos. The uncapped model cannot remain a physical fatality law past a population endpoint. Convexity gives EetR≥etER\mathbb E e^{tR}\ge e^{t\mathbb E R}EetR≥etER when the right-hand side is defined; an increase under uncertainty requires a specified ordering, such as a mean-preserving spread. Variance alone does not order arbitrary models, and a saturation cap changes convexity.

The decision question can be asked before one can estimate an average accurately.

Proposition 18 (A decision rule for reducing bounded excess harm)

Let VVV be exact Pareto with xm>0x_m>0xm​>0 and α>0\alpha>0α>0, take xm≤u<H<∞x_m\le u<H<\inftyxm​≤u<H<∞, and put X=min⁡(V,H)X=\min(V,H)X=min(V,H). Then

(X−u)+=min⁡(V,H)−min⁡(V,u).(X-u)_+=\min(V,H)-\min(V,u).(X−u)+​=min(V,H)−min(V,u).
(26)

Suppose an action costs c≥0c\ge0c≥0 in the same loss units and, by assumption, reduces this harm by a known fraction r∈[0,1]r\in[0,1]r∈[0,1]. The action has strictly smaller expected total loss exactly when

c<r E[(X−u)+].c<r\,\mathbb E[(X-u)_+].c<rE[(X−u)+​].
(27)

For any nonempty set P\mathcal PP of such loss models with the same u,H,c,ru,H,c,ru,H,c,r, the sufficient condition c<rinf⁡P∈PEP[(X−u)+]c<r\inf_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[(X-u)_+]c<rinfP∈P​EP​[(X−u)+​] makes the action preferable under every model in the set.

Proof 21

Check V≤uV\le uV≤u, u<V<Hu<V<Hu<V<H, and V≥HV\ge HV≥H to obtain the cap identity. Since 0≤(X−u)+≤H−u0\le(X-u)_+\le H-u0≤(X−u)+​≤H−u, both expected harms are finite. Subtract the no-action loss E[(X−u)+]\mathbb E[(X-u)_+]E[(X−u)+​] from c+(1−r)E[(X−u)+]c+(1-r)\mathbb E[(X-u)_+]c+(1−r)E[(X−u)+​]. This gives c−rE[(X−u)+]c-r\mathbb E[(X-u)_+]c−rE[(X−u)+​] and hence the decision rule. The infimum condition implies the strict inequality for every model.

This is a model-specific precaution calculation. It includes action costs and effectiveness; the word “uncertainty” alone does not determine either. A catastrophe-probability constraint is another possible criterion; it requires an explicitly chosen tolerance.

Use the existing pareto_capped_mean. The models share median 2 but disagree sharply about capped tail harm. The action parameters below are hypothetical loss-unit choices, not clinical effects or monetary values assigned to deaths.

Code: same median, different tail harm
from xmath.incerto.limits import pareto_capped_mean

upper, threshold, cost, reduction = 10000, 10, 5, .5
for alpha in (.6, .8, 1.2):
    xm = 2 * 2**(-1/alpha)
    harm = (pareto_capped_mean(upper, alpha, x_m=xm)
            - pareto_capped_mean(threshold, alpha, x_m=xm))
    benefit = reduction * harm
    print(f"alpha={alpha:g}: excess={harm:.2f}, benefit={benefit:.2f}, "
          f"act={benefit > cost}")

Output

alpha=0.6: excess=70.67, benefit=35.33, act=True
alpha=0.8: excess=20.57, benefit=10.28, act=True
alpha=1.2: excess=2.71, benefit=1.36, act=False

Finally, a forecast must state the action regime it assumes. Denote the future amount under action aaa by X(a)X(a)X(a) and available information by I\mathcal II. The predictive object is

P(X(a)≤x∣I).P(X(a)\le x\mid\mathcal I).P(X(a)≤x∣I).
(28)

An observed outcome after action a=1a=1a=1 does not directly test a forecast conditional on a=0a=0a=0. It also does not prove that the action caused the difference: the unobserved counterfactual needs a causal design or model. Policy feedback changes which forecast is being tested; it does not make all evaluation impossible. SCoFT v4 §§12.3–12.4, pp. 245–246, motivates this distinction. No country comparison in the source is used here as a causal estimate.
